feedback: If the child builds 34+28 from single cubes and miscounts, or insists cubes are the way even for big numbers: contrast directly with a +20-then-+8 number-line jump, showing how the representation holds the tens so the ones needn't be counted. Revisit place-value adding strategies.

If the child grabs a number line for the measuring task: sort the two problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match each tool's purpose; name what a ruler or metre stick does that a number line cannot here.

If the child reaches for a short ruler to measure the door: ask which measuring tool matches the size of the object, prompting the metre stick, so size as well as purpose drives the choice. Revisit measuring with length units.

If the child draws a number line but counts every mark in ones: model the +10 jump and ask 'can you get there in fewer jumps?', linking the tool to place-value structure rather than to the ritual of having drawn it.
Praise specifically when the child names both the efficiency gain (fewer jumps, no miscounting) and a case where the rejected tool would still win.
activities.intendedInsight: The right tool follows the PURPOSE of the problem and the size of the numbers or object, not habit: a representation that carries the tens (number line, hundred square) spares you counting ones, while a length problem needs a measuring tool matched to the object's size. Cubes remain a good fit for small numbers — this is a fit judgement, not a ranking of tools as 'babyish' or 'proper'.
learnerActions: Solve 34 + 28 using a palette of tools: cubes/base-ten, a number line, a hundred square, a ruler.
If you reach for single cubes, build and count 62 in ones — notice it is slow and easy to miscount. (Base-ten rods group the tens, so they avoid most of this counting.)
On the number line, jump 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 in two jumps.
On the hundred square (numbered with 1 at the top), add the 20 by moving two rows down to 54, then add 8 by moving forward eight squares (crossing into the next row) to reach 62.
After solving, answer: 'Why did that tool help?' and 'When would cubes actually be the better choice?'

Then tackle a measuring task: 'How long is the ribbon?' (a ruler fits, the number line does not) and 'How tall is the door?' (a metre stick fits better than a short ruler). Explain why the tool follows the problem's purpose AND the size of the object.
activities.title: Pick the tool, work the problem, justify the fit
